'''Sarah E. O'Connor''' {{post-nominals|country=GBR|FRS}} is an American natural product chemist working to understand the molecular machinery involved in assembling important plant [[natural product]]s – [[vinblastine]], [[morphine]], iridoids, [[secologanin]] – and how changing the enzymes involved in this pathway lead to diverse analogs. She was a Project Leader at the [[John Innes Centre]] in the UK between 2011 and 2019. O'Connor was appointed by the [[Max Planck Society]] in 2018 to head the Department of Natural Product Biosynthesis at the [[Max Planck Institute for Chemical Ecology]] in Jena, Germany, taking up her role during 2019.<ref>{{Cite web|url=http://www.ice.mpg.de/ext/index.php?id=shortnews2018|title=Sarah O'Connor will become new director at our institute|access-date=2018-12-20}}</ref>

== Education ==
O'Connor received her Ph.D. working with [[Barbara Imperiali]] on conformational effects induced by large proteins at the [[Massachusetts Institute of Technology]] (MIT).<ref>{{Cite journal|last=Viegas|first=J.|date=2013-12-02|title=Profile of Barbara Imperiali|journal=Proceedings of the National Academy of Sciences|language=en|volume=110|issue=52|pages=20850–20851|doi=10.1073/pnas.1321020110|pmid=24297879|pmc=3876202|bibcode=2013PNAS..11020850V |issn=0027-8424|doi-access=free}}</ref> She was a postdoctoral fellow at [[Harvard Medical School]], where she worked on epothiolone biosynthesis with Professor [[Christopher T. Walsh]] where she was first introduced to plant biochemistry.<ref>{{Cite journal|last1=O’Connor|first1=Sarah E.|last2=Chen|first2=Huawei|last3=Walsh|first3=Christopher|date=2002|title=Enzymatic Assembly of Epothilones: The EpoC Subunit and Reconstitution of the EpoA-ACP/B/C Polyketide and Nonribosomal Peptide Interfaces|journal=Biochemistry|language=EN|volume=41|issue=17|pages=5685–5694|doi=10.1021/bi020006w|pmid=11969430 }}</ref><ref name=":1">{{Cite web |title=Meet Sarah O’Connor |url=https://www.asbmb.org/asbmb-today/people/092123/meet-sarah-o-connor |access-date=2026-10-03 |website=www.asbmb.org |language=en}}</ref> She later returned to MIT as a professor from 2003 to 2010, and then from 2011 to 2019 she was Project Leader and professor in Biological Chemistry at the [[John Innes Centre]].<ref name=":0">{{Cite journal |date=2025-07-18 |title=Sarah E. O'Connor |url=https://www.wikidata.org/wiki/Q135932252 |journal=New Phytologist |volume=247 |issue=6 |pages=2514–2516 |doi=10.1111/NPH.70394}}</ref> Since 2019, she is Director of the Department of Natural Product Biosynthesis at the [[Max Planck Institute for Chemical Ecology]].<ref name=":0" />

== Research ==
O'Connor's work involves detailed study of many important species of medicinally-relevant plants: ''[[Rauvolfia serpentina]]'', ''[[Catharanthus roseus]]'',<ref name=":0" /> and ''[[Aspergillus japonicus]]''. Her lab utilizes bioinformatics and enzyme characterization to uncover new pathways by which plants construct these molecules. Insertion of new enzymes, for example a halogenase<ref>{{Cite journal|last1=Glenn|first1=Weslee S.|last2=Nims|first2=Ezekiel|last3=O’Connor|first3=Sarah E.|date=2011-12-07|title=Reengineering a Tryptophan Halogenase To Preferentially Chlorinate a Direct Alkaloid Precursor|journal=Journal of the American Chemical Society|language=EN|volume=133|issue=48|pages=19346–19349|doi=10.1021/ja2089348|pmid=22050348|issn=0002-7863}}</ref> or oxidase<ref>{{Cite journal|last1=Caputi|first1=Lorenzo|last2=Franke|first2=Jakob|last3=Farrow|first3=Scott C.|last4=Chung|first4=Khoa|last5=Payne|first5=Richard M. E.|last6=Nguyen|first6=Trinh-Don|last7=Dang|first7=Thu-Thuy T.|last8=Carqueijeiro|first8=Inês Soares Teto|last9=Koudounas|first9=Konstantinos|date=2018-05-03|title=Missing enzymes in the biosynthesis of the anticancer drug vinblastine in Madagascar periwinkle|journal=Science|volume=360|issue=6394|language=en|pages=1235–1239|doi=10.1126/science.aat4100|issn=0036-8075|pmid=29724909|bibcode=2018Sci...360.1235C |doi-access=free}}</ref> results in novel variants of the molecules not found in nature. In addition, O'Connor has started to study the molecule nepetalactone, a potential insect repellent by viewing the biosynthetic pathways of aphids with the help of etomologists.<ref name=":1" />
